concepts.name: Progressive overload
concepts.explanation: Gradually increasing the demand on muscles over time, by adding weight, reps, sets or effort, so the body keeps adapting.
concepts.caveat: Overload does not mean adding weight every session; beginners progress fast, while experienced lifters progress slowly and unevenly.
concepts.question: If you can't add weight this week, what else could count as progress?

concepts.name: Strength
concepts.explanation: The ability to produce force, usually measured as the heaviest load you can lift for one repetition (1RM) in a given exercise.
concepts.caveat: Strength is specific: a big squat does not fully transfer to other movements, speeds or joint angles.
concepts.question: Why might someone get much stronger in the first month without much bigger muscles?

concepts.name: Hypertrophy
concepts.explanation: Growth in muscle size, mainly from individual muscle fibres getting larger rather than from new fibres forming.
concepts.caveat: Visible size depends on body fat and water too, so the mirror is a noisy measure of hypertrophy.
concepts.question: Can a muscle grow while the scale weight stays the same?

concepts.name: Mechanical tension
concepts.explanation: The force muscle fibres experience while contracting against load; it is considered the main trigger for muscle growth.
concepts.caveat: "Muscle damage" and "the pump" are often assumed to drive growth, but evidence suggests they play a smaller role than tension.
concepts.question: Why can light weights lifted close to failure still build muscle?

concepts.name: Muscle protein synthesis
concepts.explanation: The process of building new muscle proteins. Training raises it for a day or two; growth happens when synthesis outpaces breakdown over time.
concepts.caveat: Short-term spikes in synthesis measured in labs do not always predict long-term muscle gain.
concepts.question: Why does one big protein meal not simply turn into muscle?

concepts.name: Training volume
concepts.explanation: The amount of work done, often counted as hard sets per muscle per week. More volume generally means more growth, up to a point.
concepts.caveat: Counting sets ignores how hard each set was; ten easy sets may do less than four hard ones.
concepts.question: At what point might adding sets stop helping and start hurting recovery?

concepts.name: Intensity
concepts.explanation: In lifting, the load as a percentage of your one-rep max. Heavier loads favour strength; a wide range of loads can build muscle.
concepts.caveat: Intensity in gyms often means "effort", which is a different thing from % of 1RM.
concepts.question: Does lifting 60% of your max for 20 reps count as high or low intensity?

concepts.name: Proximity to failure
concepts.explanation: How close a set ends to the point where you cannot complete another rep, often rated as reps in reserve (RIR).
concepts.caveat: People are poor at judging RIR, especially beginners and on high-rep sets, so "2 in reserve" is often really 5.
concepts.question: How could you check whether your estimate of reps in reserve is accurate?

concepts.name: Compound lifts
concepts.explanation: Multi-joint exercises such as squats, deadlifts, presses and rows that train several muscle groups at once.
concepts.caveat: Compound lifts are efficient but are not required; machines and isolation work can build muscle well too.
concepts.question: Which muscle might get little growth from compound lifts alone?

concepts.name: Range of motion
concepts.explanation: How far a joint moves during a rep. Training through long muscle lengths appears to be particularly good for growth.
concepts.caveat: Full range is not always better; it depends on the muscle, the exercise and any injury history.
concepts.question: Why might partial reps in a stretched position build muscle well?
phrases: range of motion hypertrophy lengthened partials
full versus partial range of motion

concepts.name: Neural adaptations
concepts.explanation: Changes in the nervous system, such as better muscle recruitment and coordination, that explain much of the early strength gain.
concepts.caveat: Neural gains are sometimes dismissed as "not real strength", but they are real and specific to the practised movement.
concepts.question: Why does strength in a new exercise rise quickly in the first few sessions?

concepts.name: Recovery
concepts.explanation: The repair and adaptation that happen between sessions; without enough of it, fatigue builds and progress stalls.
concepts.caveat: Soreness is a poor guide to recovery; you can be recovered and sore, or not recovered and not sore.
concepts.question: What signs other than soreness would tell you that you are under-recovered?

concepts.name: Protein intake
concepts.explanation: Daily protein supports muscle growth; research often points to about 1.6 g per kg of body weight per day as enough for most people.
concepts.caveat: Beyond that level extra protein adds little for most lifters, and total daily intake matters more than precise timing.
concepts.question: Does a shake right after training matter if daily protein is already high?

concepts.name: Sleep
concepts.explanation: Sleep supports recovery, hormone regulation and training performance; chronic short sleep is linked to poorer strength gains and more injuries.
concepts.caveat: Single nights of bad sleep matter less than patterns; and much of the evidence is observational.
concepts.question: How might poor sleep reduce gains even if your training plan is perfect?

concepts.name: Periodization
concepts.explanation: Planning training in phases that change volume, intensity and focus over weeks or months to manage fatigue and keep progressing.
concepts.caveat: Complex periodization models matter more for advanced athletes; beginners improve with almost any sensible plan.
concepts.question: Why might a beginner not need a detailed 12-week plan?

concepts.name: Deload
concepts.explanation: A planned short period of easier training to shed accumulated fatigue before training hard again.
concepts.caveat: Deloads are useful tools, not magic; there is little evidence for fixed schedules like every fourth week for everyone.
concepts.question: How would you decide when you need a deload instead of using a fixed calendar?
